viz.caption: Why water reads as dark: a rough surface scatters some energy back to the satellite, a smooth one mirrors it away. This is the entire physical basis of the detector — and why "dark" also catches roads, dry sand and permanent rivers, which is what forces the two-date comparison.
viz.alt: Radar pulse scatters back from rough dry ground but reflects away from smooth water, so flooded ground appears dark

rows.label: What it is
rows.body: A radar satellite that makes its own illumination, so it sees through monsoon cloud, day or night. Optical satellites cannot do this — during a flood, the sky is exactly the wrong colour.

rows.label: VV and VH
rows.body: Two ways the radar pulse comes back. VV = sent vertical, returned vertical. VH = returned horizontal, meaning something with structure — trees, walls — twisted the signal. Open water is smooth, so it mirrors the pulse away and goes dark in both.

rows.label: Why two dates
rows.body: Dark alone is not flood: roads and dry sand are dark too, rivers are always dark. You need a before and an after of the same place to find pixels that newly went dark.

viz.caption: HAND answers the only question that matters for flooding: how far must water rise from the nearest channel to reach this spot. In susceptibility.py it carries the largest weight, and the curve is calibrated so 0 m scores ~1, 8 m scores 0.5, and anything above ~25 m scores ~0.
viz.alt: Cross-section showing HAND measured as vertical height above the nearest drainage channel, low for the valley floor and high for the hillside

rows.label: What it is
rows.body: The shape of the ground. DEM is elevation. Slope is steepness. HAND — Height Above Nearest Drainage — is how high a spot sits above the nearest stream it would drain into.

rows.label: Why it is here
rows.body: It removes physically impossible answers and adds physical reasoning. Water does not sit on a 30° hillside, so a dark pixel on a steep slope is radar shadow, not flood. Low HAND means water reaches you first.

rows.label: In the repo
rows.body: Copernicus DEM GLO-30 via Planetary Computer, feeding the susceptibility surface in susceptibility.py.

viz.caption: Five lines of code, but without them the Mae Sai river is reported as a flood on every single run. The mask is JRC Global Surface Water thresholded at occurrence > 50, meaning pixels wet more than half the time in the multi-year record.
viz.alt: Detected dark pixels minus the permanent water mask equals new flooding only

rows.label: What it is
rows.body: Rainfall before the event, and a map of water that is always there — rivers, reservoirs, ponds.

rows.label: Why it is here
rows.body: Permanent water must be subtracted, or the system reports the Mae Sai river as a flood every single run. Rainfall is plausibility: heavy antecedent rain makes a detection more believable.

rows.label: The word "context"
rows.body: Deliberate. These layers are coarse and never decide anything on their own — they condition and mask.

viz.caption: Alignment is not a later resampling step — it happens at read time, which is also why only the Mae Sai window is downloaded instead of a 600 MB scene. Speckle filtering comes before differencing: SAR noise is multiplicative, so differencing raw pixels amplifies it.

rows.label: What it is
rows.body: Make the three inputs comparable. Every layer is put on the same grid, at the same resolution, in the same coordinate system, with the same maths applied every run.

rows.label: What happens
rows.body: Orbit and noise correction, calibration to real backscatter values, speckle control, terrain correction, then stacking into one layered image plus a validity mask marking unusable pixels.

rows.label: Why "canonical"
rows.body: The same recipe runs at training time and at prediction time. If those two differ even slightly, a model learns one world and is tested in another.

rows.label: Which product
rows.body: FloodGuard uses Sentinel-1 RTC products, which arrive already terrain-corrected and calibrated — so part of this step is supplied by the product rather than run in-house.

viz.caption: The actual decision function in the shipped detector — a fixed, physically anchored ramp. This is what the proposal calls "adaptive Otsu"; it is not. An Otsu threshold would be recomputed per scene from the histogram, moving with each acquisition. This one does not move, which is arguably the stronger property.
viz.alt: Flood probability as a function of decibel drop: flat at zero below 1 dB, rising linearly to 1 at 5 dB, with the binary cut at 0.5 falling at 3 dB

rows.label: What it does
rows.body: Converts both dates to decibels, subtracts after from before, and maps the drop onto a 0–1 probability with a fixed physical ramp: a 1 dB drop is dry, a 5 dB drop is certainly flooded, and 0.5 is the cut.

rows.label: The maths
rows.body: combined = 0.6 · VH_drop + 0.4 · VV_drop

rows.label: Why VH is heavier
rows.body: Vegetation and buildings depolarize strongly, so their VH is high. Losing it under water is a bigger, cleaner signal than the VV drop.

rows.label: Not a model
rows.body: This is a deterministic statistical method. Nothing is trained, nothing is learned. It is transparent and it always runs — which is precisely why it is the baseline everything else must beat.

rows.label: Executed result
rows.body: 0.21% of Mae Sai district newly flooded on the 15 Sep acquisition.

viz.caption: The four factors plotted from the real coefficients in the source. Each is a physical statement, not a fitted parameter: half-response at 8 m above drainage, 600 m from a channel, and 5° of slope. This is what scores AUC 0.74 — and why a tree ensemble would add opacity without adding evidence.
viz.alt: Three response curves: HAND falls to half at 8 metres, distance to river decays to near zero by 1.5 kilometres, slope falls to half at 5 degrees

rows.label: What it does
rows.body: Decision-tree ensembles take the radar change plus terrain, drainage and land cover, and learn which combinations really mean flood. Interpretable — you can ask which feature drove each prediction.

rows.label: Benchmark result
rows.body: XGBoost IoU 0.868, F1 0.929, precision 0.913, recall 0.946, ECE 0.040. Random Forest is marginally ahead at IoU 0.869. Both are well calibrated at full coverage.

rows.label: Beats the baseline
rows.body: Decisively — the VH-Otsu baseline scores IoU 0.233 on the same split. That satisfies our promotion criterion on the benchmark.

rows.label: Still gated for Mae Sai
rows.body: Mae Sai inference exists per model but carries evidence_tier: candidate, can_feed_decision_layer: false, and claims no Mae Sai accuracy. The terrain susceptibility index (AUC 0.74) remains the training-free fallback.

viz.caption: The U-Net was not the failure — its supervision was. Registration error was ruled out as the benign explanation: agreement only reaches 0.081 even at 3-pixel tolerance, and 79% of the reference survives 1-pixel erosion.
viz.alt: Area-proportional diagram: the MNDWI training label covers 8.7 times the reference water area while overlapping only half of it

rows.label: What it is
rows.body: Image-segmentation networks that label every pixel flood or not-flood, learning shape and texture rather than one brightness cut-off. U-Net compresses the image then rebuilds it at full resolution; FPN reads several scales at once.

rows.label: Benchmark result
rows.body: SAR arm IoU 0.370 (F1 0.540, precision 0.788, recall 0.411, ECE 0.205). Context arm, with terrain and land cover added, improves markedly to IoU 0.703 (F1 0.825, ECE 0.063).

rows.label: It loses to the trees
rows.body: XGBoost and Random Forest reach IoU ~0.87 on the same split. This reproduces a published finding (Li et al., 2023): deep nets do not automatically beat tree ensembles for pixel-level flood mapping.

rows.label: What it carries
rows.body: Not a yes/no map. Four things: probability per pixel, validity (was this pixel observable at all), uncertainty, and abstention — the right to say "not sure here" instead of guessing.

rows.label: Why abstention matters
rows.body: A model that must answer everywhere is forced to guess in radar shadow and dense city. One that can decline gives a smaller, more trustworthy map.

rows.label: What it means
rows.body: The work is not deleted or hidden. It is published, inspectable, and carries the named reason it was refused. It simply has no influence.

rows.label: Why this is a feature
rows.body: Most rapid-mapping products handle limitations with a disclaimer printed after the recommendation. Here the limitation decides whether the recommendation can be made at all.

viz.caption: The two halves of the scoring policy in one picture: a published, re-weightable index on top, and the override that outranks it below. Flood likelihood carries the largest weight, which is precisely why the AI feeding it must pass the gate first.
viz.alt: The five FPPS weights drawn to scale, and the low-confidence override that sends Ko Chang's score of 44 to class E

rows.label: Exposure
rows.body: How many people are under the water. The beginning of the analysis, not the end of it.

rows.label: Road risk
rows.body: Which roads likely became impassable, scored from flood evidence, road class and bridge context. An estimate, never a report of an actual closure.

rows.label: Access loss
rows.body: Shortest-path routing run twice — normal network, then disrupted network. A person counts as losing access only if they could reach a hospital or shelter within 15/30/60 minutes before, and cannot after.

rows.label: Equity gap
rows.body: The signature output. Compare the access-loss rate of a declared vulnerable group against a comparison group: the difference in percentage points and the ratio. Today the Mae Sai group split is a terrain/remoteness proxy — not age-resolved, and must not be described as older-adult vulnerability.

rows.label: FPPS and A–E
rows.body: One score from five weighted components, mapped to five action classes. Low confidence forces Class E regardless of how high the number is.

rows.label: Public
rows.body: Thai-first preparedness for residents. Reduced evidence set, unverified facilities withheld, no evacuation instructions issued.

rows.label: Command
rows.body: Government and rescue. Priority ranking with score components and confidence on every rank; candidate road risk always labelled separately from confirmed conditions.

rows.label: Studio
rows.body: Reviewers and technical staff. Gate status with exact block reasons, run receipts, and whether each artifact may feed the decision layer.

rows.label: The key point
rows.body: Three controlled interpretations of one evidence context — enforced in code, not in layout. Not one dashboard in three skins.

title: What these numbers do and do not say

rows.label: Trees win
rows.body: XGBoost and Random Forest are near-identical and beat the Otsu baseline by 0.64 IoU. They are also well calibrated (ECE ~0.04): when they say 70%, they mean it.

rows.label: The baseline’s shape
rows.body: Otsu has precision 0.884 but recall 0.241 — it finds only the most obvious water, and is right when it speaks. That is a defensible baseline, not a broken one.

rows.label: Deep learning loses
rows.body: U-Net trails badly on SAR alone (0.370) and improves a lot with terrain context (0.703), but still loses to the trees. This matches Li et al. (2023), which the proposal already cites. Say so plainly.

rows.label: What it is not
rows.body: These are benchmark numbers. Every Mae Sai artifact still carries evidence_tier: candidate, can_feed_decision_layer: false, and the explicit assumption that no qualified Thai reference exists, so no Mae Sai accuracy is claimed.

viz.caption: The current Mae Sai state, drawn honestly. Two criteria pass, three do not, and one failure is enough — there is no partial credit and no "use it with a caveat" path.
viz.alt: Five promotion criteria feed one gate; four pass but the reference requirement fails, so the flood map is routed to blocked rather than into the decision layer
